In [[mathematics]], a function <math>f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} </math> is '''symmetrically continuous''' at a point ''x'' if
<math display="block">\lim_{h\to 0} f(x+h)-f(x-h) = 0.</math>

The usual definition of [[continuous function|continuity]] implies symmetric continuity, but the converse is not true. For example, the function <math>x^{-2}</math> is symmetrically continuous at <math>x=0</math>, but not continuous.

Also, [[Symmetric derivative|symmetric differentiability]] implies symmetric continuity, but the converse is not true just like usual continuity does not imply differentiability.

The set of the symmetrically continuous functions, with the usual [[scalar multiplication]] can be easily shown to have the structure of a [[vector space]] over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, similarly to the usually continuous functions, which form a [[linear subspace]] within it.
